item.title: Kevin Warsh Just Told Congress Inflation Will Be a 'Thing of the Past'
item.description:
It took just six words for the new Federal Reserve chairman to rattle Wall Street: “The Committee will deliver price stability.”

That was Kevin Warsh in his first policy statement, and on July 14, 2026, he doubled down before Congress — promising lawmakers that inflation will soon be a “thing of the past.” For a market that assumed a friendlier Fed was coming, the message landed like cold water.

So who is Kevin Warsh, why is his blunt approach spooking investors, and what does it mean for your wallet? Let’s break it down.

item.title: Mortgage Refinance Rates: The Surprising 2026 Shift
item.description:
Here’s a number that stopped homeowners in their tracks this spring: mortgage refinance demand dropped 18% in a single stretch as rates climbed to their highest level since August. Then, almost as quickly, the story flipped.

By the end of June 2026, the 30-year mortgage rate had fallen to its lowest point since May. If you own a home and have been waiting on the sidelines, the ground just moved under your feet.

item.title: Powell Speech at Harvard: Fed Chair Signals 'Wait and See' Amid Inflation-Growth Dilemma
item.description:
Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell just told markets exactly what they feared — and needed — to hear: the Fed is in no rush to cut rates, even as the economy faces mounting headwinds from war, surging oil prices, and stubborn inflation.

Key Takeaways

  • Powell spoke at Harvard on March 30, 2026, in a moderated discussion with economics students
  • The Fed held rates steady at 3.5%–3.75% for the second consecutive meeting on March 18
  • CME FedWatch shows a 95.3% probability of no change at the April 29 meeting
  • Brent crude has surged to $114 amid the US-Israel-Iran conflict
  • The dot plot still projects just one rate cut for 2026

Powell’s Harvard Appearance: More Than a Classroom Visit

What was officially billed as a moderated discussion with an undergraduate economics class at Harvard University quickly became one of the most closely watched Fed events of the year. Beginning at 10:30 AM Eastern on March 30, the session was livestreamed on the Federal Reserve’s official YouTube channel.
